For opening argument: ## Opening argument: Islam permits music

Honourable judges and respected opponents: the proposition before us is not “Does Islam permit every lyric, every concert, and every lifestyle associated with music?” Of course not. Islam forbids obscenity, intoxication, sexual immorality, mockery of religion, and anything that leads people away from their obligations. The real question is: **Does Islam prohibit music as a category?** The answer is no. Islam permits music and singing when their content, setting, and effects remain within Islamic ethics.

The starting point in Islamic law is that worldly things are permissible unless there is clear evidence prohibiting them. The Qur’an warns believers not to invent prohibitions in Allah’s name:  

> “O you who believe, do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.” — Qur’an 5:87  

And:  

> “Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?” — Qur’an 7:32  

So if someone claims that all music is haram, the burden of proof is on them to show a clear, general, and decisive prohibition. But the Qur’an contains no explicit verse saying “music is haram.” Verses sometimes cited, such as “idle talk” in Qur’an 31:6, are not explicit; they condemn speech or entertainment that misleads people from Allah, not every melody, rhythm, or instrument.

More importantly, the Sunnah shows that the Prophet ﷺ allowed singing and percussion in lawful settings. In an authentic hadith, two young girls were singing in the house of Aisha رضي الله عنها on Eid. Abu Bakr objected, calling it “the instruments of Satan,” but the Prophet ﷺ corrected him and said:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 952; Sahih Muslim 892

This is a decisive point. If singing were inherently haram, the Prophet ﷺ would not have allowed it in his own house, on Eid, in the presence of his wife. He did not say, “Music is forbidden.” He said, in effect, that lawful joy has a place in Islam.

Likewise, at weddings, the Prophet ﷺ encouraged public celebration. When Aisha arranged a marriage among the Ansar, the Prophet ﷺ asked:

> “O Aisha, was there any amusement? For the Ansar like amusement.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 5162

In another narration, girls beat the duff and sang at a wedding in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. He did not forbid the singing or the drum; he only corrected one lyric that attributed knowledge of the unseen to him.  
— Sahih al-Bukhari 5147

This shows the Islamic principle clearly: **the problem is not melody, rhythm, or singing itself; the problem is unlawful content.** The Prophet ﷺ corrected the lyric, not the music.

The opposing side may cite the hadith mentioning people who will “make lawful” wine, silk, zina and *ma‘azif* — musical instruments. — Sahih al-Bukhari 5590. But this narration must be understood alongside the other authentic narrations where the Prophet ﷺ permitted singing and the duff. Therefore it cannot mean a blanket prohibition of every form of music in every circumstance. At most, it condemns musical entertainment associated with wine, sexual immorality, arrogance, and heedlessness — exactly the kinds of settings Islam already forbids.

This balanced view is not a modern invention. Major scholars held that listening to pleasant sounds is not automatically forbidden. Imam al-Ghazali devoted a section of *Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din* to *sama‘* — listening to song and melody — and argued that beautiful sounds are not haram in themselves; they become haram because of external factors such as immoral lyrics, lustful contexts, or neglect of duties. Ibn Hazm likewise argued in *al-Muhalla* that there is no sound, decisive text prohibiting singing as such. Al-Shawkani also rejected the claim that there is scholarly consensus on a blanket prohibition of music.

So the correct Islamic position is principled and balanced: music is permitted when it is clean in content, lawful in setting, and does not lead to sin or neglect of obligations. Islam is not a religion that bans beauty, joy, rhythm, poetry, or celebration. It regulates them. The Prophet ﷺ allowed lawful celebration on Eid and at weddings. Therefore, the proposition stands: **Islam permits music — not without limits, but certainly in principle.**

## Key citations

- Qur’an 5:87 — “Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.”  
- Qur’an 7:32 — “Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah… and the good things of provision?”  
- Qur’an 31:6 — Condemns “idle talk” that misleads from Allah; not an explicit prohibition of all music.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 952; Sahih Muslim 892 — The Prophet ﷺ allowed girls to sing on Eid in Aisha’s house.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5162 — The Prophet ﷺ asked whether there was amusement at an Ansari wedding.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5147 — Girls sang and beat the duff at a wedding; the Prophet ﷺ corrected only an improper lyric.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5590 — Hadith mentioning *ma‘azif*, interpreted by permissive scholars as referring to sinful musical gatherings, not every form of music.  
- Al-Ghazali, *Ihya’ ‘Ulum al-Din*, “Kitab Adab al-Sama‘ wa’l-Wajd” — Argues that listening to beautiful sounds is not intrinsically forbidden.  
- Ibn Hazm, *al-Muhalla* — Argues against a blanket prohibition of singing.  
- Al-Shawkani, *Nayl al-Awtar* and his treatise rejecting claimed consensus on prohibiting all *sama‘* — Notes disagreement among scholars and rejects a universal ban.

Opponent's argument: **Opening argument against the proposition “Islam permits music”**

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful.

I stand against the proposition that Islam generally permits music. The more accurate statement is that Islamic law permits limited, defined forms of vocal celebration—such as the duff at weddings or Eid—while the mainstream classical position prohibits musical instruments and entertainment-singing that distracts from obedience to Allah, stirs desire, or becomes a vehicle of heedlessness.

The first point is that the strongest textual evidence is not neutral. The Prophet ﷺ explicitly foretold that people from his Ummah would “regard as lawful” certain things that are in fact unlawful, and he included **musical instruments** among them:

> “There will be among my Ummah people who will regard as lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590**

This hadith is central because musical instruments are listed alongside matters whose prohibition is agreed upon: zina and wine. The phrase “will regard as lawful” indicates that these things are not lawful to begin with. Classical scholars such as Ibn Hajar al-‘Asqalani discussed this narration as evidence against musical instruments in *Fath al-Bari*.

Second, the Qur’an condemns forms of entertainment that divert people from Allah’s path:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead others from the way of Allah without knowledge and takes it in ridicule. For such there will be a humiliating punishment.”  
> — **Qur’an 31:6**

Several early authorities interpreted “idle talk” here as singing. Ibn Mas‘ud, one of the greatest companions and Qur’anic scholars, reportedly said regarding this verse: “By Allah, it refers to singing.” This interpretation is cited in major tafsir works, including **Tafsir al-Tabari** and **Tafsir Ibn Kathir** under Qur’an 31:6.

Third, Islam’s moral framework does not judge entertainment merely by whether it feels harmless. It asks: What does it cultivate in the heart? Does it increase remembrance of Allah, modesty, and discipline—or does it normalize desire, vanity, intoxication of the emotions, and heedlessness? Much of what is called music is inseparable from precisely those harms: sensuality, pride, vulgarity, addiction, and distraction from prayer and Qur’an.

Fourth, the existence of exceptions proves restriction, not blanket permission. Yes, there are authentic reports of young girls singing with the **duff** on Eid in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ:

> Abu Bakr objected, calling it “the instruments of Satan,” but the Prophet ﷺ said: “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 952; Sahih Muslim, no. 892**

But this narration concerns young girls, simple singing, and the duff on Eid. It does not establish permission for all instruments, all musical gatherings, or commercialized entertainment. In Islamic law, a specific concession does not erase a general prohibition.

Similarly, the Prophet ﷺ allowed the duff in marriage celebrations:

> “Publicize this marriage and beat the duff for it.”  
> — Reported in **Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, no. 1089** and **Sunan Ibn Majah, no. 1895**, with supporting narrations

Again, this supports a limited exception, not a general rule that music is permissible.

The mainstream classical position of the four legal schools was therefore not that “music is simply halal.” Rather, they generally prohibited musical instruments, while allowing limited exceptions such as the duff in weddings and Eid, and permitting permissible poetry or chanting without unlawful content or instruments. Scholars differed over details, but the claim that Islam broadly permits music is not supported by the strongest hadith evidence or by the dominant juristic tradition.

So my argument is simple: if Islam had intended to permit music generally, we would not find musical instruments condemned in authentic hadith, interpreted negatively by leading companions, and restricted by jurists to narrow exceptions. Islam does not close the door to joy, celebration, poetry, or beauty—but it does regulate entertainment so that the heart remains attached to Allah, not to heedlessness.

Therefore, the proposition “Islam permits music” is too broad and misleading. The sounder position is that Islam permits limited forms of lawful vocal expression and specific ceremonial use of the duff, while musical instruments and music associated with distraction, desire, or sinful environments are prohibited or, at minimum, deeply restricted.

For opening argument: Madam Chair, respected judges, and colleagues:

I stand for the proposition that **Islam promotes women’s rights**—not as a slogan, but as a claim grounded in its foundational texts and early practice. The question is not whether every Muslim society has always lived up to Islam’s ideals; clearly, many have not. The question is what Islam itself teaches. And on that question, the evidence is strong: Islam affirms women’s spiritual equality, protects their legal and economic personhood, regulates family life through consent and mutual obligation, and recognizes women as active moral members of society.

First, Islam establishes the equal human and spiritual worth of women and men. The Qur’an states that all human beings are created from “a single soul” (Qur’an 4:1). It repeatedly addresses men and women together as equally accountable before God: “The believing men and believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong” (Qur’an 9:71). Another verse lists Muslim men and women, believing men and women, truthful men and women, patient men and women, and concludes that God has prepared for all of them forgiveness and great reward (Qur’an 33:35). This is a profound moral foundation: women are not spiritually inferior, not morally secondary, and not excluded from religious responsibility or reward.

Second, Islam gave women independent legal and economic rights. The Qur’an explicitly grants women the right to own and benefit from property: “For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned” (Qur’an 4:32). It grants women inheritance rights: “For men is a share of what parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share” (Qur’an 4:7). In a world where many women were treated as property, Islam declared that women could inherit property. The Qur’an also condemns the practice of inheriting women against their will and commands men to live with women honorably: “It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion… live with them in kindness” (Qur’an 4:19).

Third, Islam protects women’s rights in marriage and family life. Marriage in Islam is not ownership; it is a covenant based on tranquility, mercy, and love: “He created for you spouses… and placed between you affection and mercy” (Qur’an 30:21). The Prophet Muhammad taught that women’s consent matters in marriage: “A previously married woman should not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin should not be married until her permission is sought” (Sahih al-Bukhari 5136; Sahih Muslim 1419). The Qur’an also commands fairness in divorce and prohibits harming women to coerce them: “Do not retain them to harm them” (Qur’an 2:231). These are not minor points; they are protections of dignity, consent, and security.

Fourth, Islam promotes women’s education, public participation, and social dignity. The Prophet said, “Women are the twin halves of men” (Sunan Abi Dawud 236; Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 113). He also said, “Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from going to the mosques” (Sahih al-Bukhari 900; Sahih Muslim 442), showing that women were not to be excluded from communal religious life. Women participated in pledges of allegiance to the Prophet, a form of public and political recognition, as indicated in Qur’an 60:12. The Qur’an even preserves the case of a woman who challenged an unjust marital custom, and God responded to her complaint directly: “God has certainly heard the speech of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband” (Qur’an 58:1). That is a striking affirmation that a woman’s voice, grievance, and legal claim matter.

Finally, Islam elevates women in their roles as mothers without reducing them to motherhood alone. The Prophet was asked who deserves the best companionship, and he answered, “Your mother,” then again “Your mother,” then again “Your mother,” and only then “Your father” (Sahih al-Bukhari 5971; Sahih Muslim 2548). The Qur’an similarly commands gratitude and kindness to parents while specifically recognizing the hardship borne by mothers (Qur’an 31:14; 46:15).

So the proposition is not that Muslim communities have always been perfect. They have not. The proposition is that Islam itself promotes women’s rights—and its sources demonstrate that it does. Islam affirms women as full moral agents before God, grants them property and inheritance rights, requires consent in marriage, protects them from abuse and coercion, honors their voices in public and private life, and commands men to treat them with justice and kindness.

That is why I affirm: **Islam promotes women’s rights.**

Opponent's argument: **Opening argument against the proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”**

Islam may have improved some women’s conditions in 7th-century Arabia—for example by recognizing women’s inheritance and condemning female infanticide. But **granting limited protections in a patriarchal society is not the same as promoting equal rights.** The central problem is that Islamic scripture and traditional jurisprudence repeatedly place women in a legally and socially subordinate position to men.

In inheritance, the Qur’an states that “the male shall have the equal of the portion of two females” in a core inheritance rule.¹ In financial testimony, the Qur’an instructs that if two male witnesses are not available, then one man and two women may testify, “so that if one of the two women errs, the other can remind her.”² These are not marginal details; they concern property, courts, and legal credibility.

Qur’an 4:34 says men are “in charge of” women and describes righteous women as obedient; it also permits husbands, in cases of marital disobedience, to admonish wives, separate from them in bed, and “strike” or “beat” them, depending on translation.³ Qur’an 2:228 says men have “a degree” over women.⁴ A rights-promoting system does not make one sex the manager, disciplinarian, and superior of the other.

Fourth, canonical hadith literature reinforces women’s subordinate status. Sahih al-Bukhari records Muhammad as saying that a people who appoint a woman as ruler “will never succeed.”⁷ Another hadith describes women as “deficient in intelligence and religion,” explaining this deficiency partly by reference to women’s testimony being treated as half that of men in certain cases.⁸ A further hadith says that if a wife refuses her husband’s call to bed, angels curse her until morning.⁹ These texts have shaped centuries of legal and cultural attitudes toward women’s authority, credibility, and sexual autonomy.

Islam’s traditional framework gives women some protections, but within a hierarchy controlled by men.

Therefore, while many Muslims today sincerely reinterpret their faith in egalitarian ways, those reforms often succeed by moving beyond or softening the plain meaning of classical rules—not because the traditional system itself is built on women’s equality. Honourable judges, colleagues, and audience:

The proposition before us is simple: **Muslims can be active citizens in secular countries.** I support it because both Islamic principle and real-world experience show that Muslims can participate fully, loyally, and constructively in secular democracies.

First, we should define our terms. A *secular country* is not necessarily an anti-religious country. At its best, secularism means that the state does not belong to one church, mosque, synagogue, or temple; it belongs equally to all citizens. It protects freedom of conscience, allows different communities to live together, and asks citizens to work through common laws and democratic institutions. That is not a threat to Muslim citizenship—it is often the very framework that allows Muslims to practice their faith freely.

Islamic ethics strongly support active citizenship. The Qur’an commands believers to stand for justice even when it is difficult: *“O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for God, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives”* (Qur’an 4:135). It also says: *“Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness”* (Qur’an 5:8). These are not instructions for isolation or passivity. They are instructions for moral engagement. In a modern secular country, voting, serving on local councils, joining school boards, working in public service, defending civil liberties, paying taxes, volunteering, and speaking out against injustice are all ways of fulfilling that ethical duty.

Second, Islam recognizes peaceful coexistence with people of other faiths. The Qur’an states: *“God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes”* (Qur’an 60:8). It also declares, *“There is no compulsion in religion”* (Qur’an 2:256). These verses are deeply compatible with citizenship in plural societies. They support the idea that Muslims can live alongside non-Muslims not merely as tolerated minorities, but as neighbours, colleagues, voters, public servants, and partners in the common good.

Third, citizenship involves a covenant: an agreement to respect the law, protect the rights of others, and contribute to society. Islamic teaching places great weight on honouring agreements. The Qur’an says, *“O you who believe, fulfil your contracts”* (Qur’an 5:1). A well-known prophetic teaching states that Muslims are bound by their conditions and agreements, so long as those agreements do not require sin or injustice. This means that when Muslims live as citizens or lawful residents in a country, they have a religious as well as civic obligation to act responsibly, honestly, and peacefully.

Nor is this only theory. Islamic history contains examples of plural political life. The early community in Medina included Muslims and Jewish tribes in a shared civic arrangement often referred to as the Constitution of Medina. While historians debate details of the document, it is widely cited as an early example of a political community in which different religious groups retained their religious identity while sharing mutual civic obligations. That example matters because it shows that Muslim political thought has never been limited to one narrow model of society.

And in the modern world, the evidence is visible everywhere. Muslims serve as doctors, soldiers, teachers, judges, police officers, civil servants, elected representatives, charity workers, journalists, and community organizers in secular countries. They have served in parliaments and city halls, led major cities, defended their countries, and contributed to science, business, culture, and public life. In the United States, Pew Research Center has found that the overwhelming majority of Muslims say they are proud to be American, while also maintaining their religious identity. That is exactly what active citizenship looks like: belonging to one’s country without abandoning one’s conscience.

The opposing side may argue that Muslims cannot be active citizens because their ultimate moral loyalty is to God. But this misunderstands both religion and citizenship. Many Christians, Jews, Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, and others also hold ultimate religious commitments while serving faithfully in secular democracies. A secular state does not require citizens to have no religion; it requires them to respect equal citizenship and the rule of law. Muslims can do that. Indeed, Islamic principles of justice, mercy, trustworthiness, consultation, and covenant-keeping encourage them to do so.

So the question is not whether Muslims can be active citizens in secular countries. They already are. The deeper question is whether secular societies will live up to their own principles by welcoming the full participation of all citizens, including Muslims. A confident democracy should not fear Muslim participation; it should welcome it. Muslim citizens, like all citizens, can help build safer neighbourhoods, fairer laws, stronger institutions, and more compassionate societies.
